title: Gating cost accounting + long‑context experiments
content:
Summary:

These are working notes for profiling and attributing latency/cost when top-k gating and dynamic expert prefetch interact with KV cache and long contexts (32k+ tokens). Focus models: Llama-Variant-70B (dense), Mistral-70B (dense), Qwen-MoE-110B (experimental MoE gating). Goal is to build an accounting model that explains per-request p50/p95/p99 CPU+GPU host time and remote memcpy overhead in terms of: gate compute, routing fanout, prefetch IO, KV cache misses, and attention recompute.

Motivation / Motivation evidence:
- Customer A reported P99 spikes for few long-chat flows; traces show a sudden ~40–150ms additional wall time for some tokens when routing fanout > 16.
- Correlating traces with eviction metrics shows these requests had repeated KV cache misses for the same sequence fragment (hot prefix with interleaved retrievals).
- Hypothesis: gating decisions that route to many experts increase prefetch churn and cause increased PCIe transfers when KV cache entries are cold/fragmented, amplifying latency in long-context workloads.

Quick summary of what we ran (configs):
- Models: llamav-70b-dense, mistral-70b, qwen-110b-moe (4k/32k variants).
- Context lengths: 4k baseline, 16k mid, 32k stress.
- Routing: top-2 deterministic / top-2 softmax-probs thresholded at 0.05 / top-4 capped by capacity factor 1.2 / topk-sampling (degenerate).
- Prefetch policies: none, eager (prefetch full expert activations on gate decision), deferred (trigger prefetch once decoder crosses token t+8), demand (on miss + async backpressure).
- Batching: 1 (single-stream) / 8 (small batch) / 32 (server batch) representative of our serving modes.

Representative observations (numbers are wall-clock per-token on A100-like node, median of 200 samples):
- Llamav-70b-dense, 4k context, batch=1: p50=45ms, p95=72ms. 32k context: p50=58ms, p95=110ms. 
- Mistral-70b, 32k context, batch=1: p50=52ms, p95=95ms.
- Qwen-110b-MoE, top-2, eager prefetch, 32k, batch=1: p50=65ms, p95=180ms, p99=420ms (heavy tail correlated with routing fanout > 24 and repeated KV miss).

Breakdown attribution (approx, from sampled CPU/GPU perf counters + async memcpy tracing):
- Gate forward (CPU/GPU mixed): 1.5–6ms depending on gating implementation and whether routing table lookup hits L2.
- Routing serialization + queueing (host): 2–12ms (spikes when we serialize per-expert RPCs rather than multi-expert fused dispatch).
- Prefetch memcpy (GPU<->host) per expert: 0.8–3.0ms (depends on activation size, quantization); for fanout 16 with eager prefetch ~20–40ms added.
- KV cache lookup and reconstruction (GPU kernels): 3–18ms depending on cache locality and sharded layout.
- Attention recompute (long-context attention windows + chunking): 6–40ms increase moving from 4k to 32k with current tiling scheme.

Key diagnostic traces and what they mean:
- Trace INF-TRACE-20241112-13: long-running request where gate picks 28 experts across two workers. We saw backpressure on the router queue; the dispatcher serialized 28 memcpy calls instead of fused vectorized dispatch because per-expert payloads were variable size -> big tail.
- Trace INF-TRACE-20241127-07: batch=8 case where one sample causes eviction storms (hot prefix + repeated cross-sample reuse) causing p99 to blow up. Root cause was mixing LRU-ish ring buffer with inconsistent alignment causing full page memcpy instead of partial (we copy whole tile on miss).

What surprised us:
- Eager prefetch helps throughput under stable low-fanout (<8) cases but makes tail latency worse once fanout increases or eviction increases. The extra bytes moved amplify p99 more than p50.
- Some Qwen MoE gating implementations do a host-side softmax then topk which is cheap, but the ensuing per-expert bookkeeping (capacity checks) is the main host-side cost and scales super-linearly when many requests overlap.
- In one experiment, enabling quantized expert activations (8-bit) reduced memcpy per expert by ~2.8× and trimmed p99 by ~18% for fanout-heavy traces.

Suggested mitigations to test (ordered):
1) Fused multi-expert dispatch: build a fused memcpy path that concatenates per-expert payloads for a request and performs a single vectorized transfer where possible. Should reduce serialization cost for variable sized activations.
2) Adaptive prefetch policy: prefetch only when (estimated_fanout * activation_size) < threshold AND (recent_cache_miss_rate < 0.1). Otherwise fallback to demand prefetch with prioritized async queue.
3) Incremental KV lookup: instead of reconstructing full activation on miss, stream partial tiles needed for the next N tokens to overlap compute and IO. Requires attention kernel to support micro-chunks.
4) Gate-level local short-circuit: if a gate's top2 experts have nearly identical logits and both are warm in the same shard, prefer local-expert routing to avoid cross-shard traffic.
5) Quantized activation spill policy: store cold activations on host in 8-bit layout and only convert to fp16 on GPU when required. Reduced host->GPU bandwidth in our tests.

Open experiments / TODOs:
- [ ] Run fused-memcopy prototype (branch: perf/fused-dispatch-2024) against long-tail workload generator. Patch in perf harness.
- [ ] Measure impact of alignment/padding optimizations on memcpy patterns (root cause of full-page copying in trace INF-TRACE-20241127-07).
- [ ] Re-run with realistic customer prompt set (Customer-A-chatset v2) to get more representative p99 numbers.
- [ ] Investigate hybrid gating (topk + capacity-aware soft cutoff) and measure host CPU pressure.
- [ ] Add per-request 'estimated bytes to prefetch' metric to trace headers for offline correlation.

Notes on measurement methodology (lessons learned):
- Don’t rely only on kernel-level profilers (nvprof/nsys). They miss host-side serialization and async memcpy overlapped with compute; we instrumented at dispatcher boundary (tracepoints in C++) and correlate with GPU timestamp markers to get holistic attribution.
- Synthetic long-context tokens (repeating token patterns) biased cache behavior; we used a mixing strategy: 70% real prompts, 30% long synthetic expansions to stress prefixes.
- Batch mixing matters: multi-stream small-batch interleaving increases effective fanout because different samples hit disjoint expert sets. Keep a separate harness for single-stream and server-batch scenarios.

Implementation notes for the runtime team:
- Router: add a compact per-request 'fanout_estimate' field to route meta. Use it to short-circuit eager prefetch decisions. (PR: github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/1432)
- Dispatcher: add a coalesce buffer for small expert payloads; flush thresholds: 1MB or 32 experts. Configurable via runtime flags.
- KV cache: adopt page-level validity bits to avoid full-tile copies on partial misses. This requires updating attention/kV accessors to support partial tile assembly.

Risks and tradeoffs:
- Fused dispatch increases memory coalescing but complicates per-expert retry semantics (what if one expert compute fails or OOMs?). Need transactional behavior or a fallback path.
- Prefetch conservative thresholds could reduce throughput in common low-fanout cases. Must be adaptive and use lightweight estimators.
- Quantization of cold activations can introduce accuracy regressions; need offline QA on per-task downstream metrics and targeted evals.

Appendix: quick command snippets used in runs:
- Run harness (single-stream, trace mode): ./perf/harness --model qwen-110b-moe --context 32768 --batch 1 --routing top2 --prefetch eager --tracefile /tmp/trace.json
- Extract memcpy events (local script): python tools/trace_parser.py /tmp/trace.json --filter memcpy --group-by expert_id --out /tmp/memstats.csv

References / links:
- PERF PR: github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/1432 (fused dispatch sketch)
- Jira: INF-7923 long-context moe p99 investigation (internal ticket)
- Confluence note: confluence.redwood/gating-playbook (gating heuristics and control knobs)

Concluding thoughts (short):
We can explain a significant portion of tail latency via routing-induced IO amplification (prefetch+memcpy) plus KV cache miss storms. Prioritizing fused dispatch and adaptive prefetch looks like the highest ROI path. Next steps are to prototype fused dispatch and add per-request byte estimates to traces so we have a better signal for adaptive policies.

-- Aisha
